summary: Spatial aptitude asks you to move shapes in your head: reflect, rotate, translate and scale figures, read mirror and water images, fold nets into cubes, track dice, and unfold punched paper. Almost every question reduces to a small set of rules: coordinate rules for transformations, the painted-cube counts, Euler's formula, the opposite-face rules for nets and dice, and reverse unfolding one crease at a time. Sketch on the scratch pad and track one asymmetric feature instead of the whole figure.
highYield: Painted cube counts: 8 corners, 12(n − 2) edge cubes, 6(n − 2)² face cubes and (n − 2)³ hidden cubes; a 1-mark NAT.
Opposite face from two dice views with one common face: list both views clockwise from the common face and pair matching positions.
Which cube folds from a net: alternate squares in a straight run and the ends of a Z-shaped four are opposite, so they can never be shown side by side.
Unfolding a punched sheet: reflect each hole across the last crease first; k folds turn one interior hole into 2^k holes.
Mirror image reverses left and right, water image reverses top and bottom; a mirror also reverses the order of letters in a word.

topics.title: Reflection across axes and the diagonal lines
points: A reflection flips a figure across a mirror line: every point moves to the same distance on the other side, along a perpendicular to the line.

Coordinate rules: x-axis (x, y) → (x, −y); y-axis (x, y) → (−x, y); line y = x (x, y) → (y, x); line y = −x (x, y) → (−y, −x); the point reflection in the origin, (x, y) → (−x, −y), is the same map as the 180° rotation and keeps orientation.
For a line reflection, points on the mirror line stay fixed, and distances and angles are preserved, but the orientation reverses: a clockwise-labelled triangle ABC becomes anticlockwise.
Because a reflection reverses orientation, no rotation can produce it. If an option equals the original figure turned over, it is a reflection, not a rotation.

lesson.why: Reflection questions ask where a point or shape lands after a flip. One wrong sign in a coordinate rule, or mistaking a flip for a turn, picks the wrong option.
lesson.intro: A reflection flips a figure over a mirror line. Each point goes to the other side of the line, the same distance away, along a path that meets the line at a right angle. Points on the line do not move. Lengths and angles stay the same, but the figure comes out turned over, like your left hand seen in a mirror.

definitions.meaning: The line the figure is flipped across; its points stay fixed.
A clockwise ordering of labelled corners becomes anticlockwise after a reflection.

principle.text: Across the x-axis only the sign of $y$ changes, and across the y-axis only the sign of $x$ changes. Across $y=x$ the coordinates swap. Across $y=-x$ they swap and both change sign.

lesson.limits: These rules hold for mirror lines through the origin. A mirror such as $x=2$ needs the distance to the line: the image of $(x,y)$ is $(4-x,y)$. Reflection cannot be built from a single rotation, since it reverses orientation.

example.problem: Reflect the point $(3,-2)$ in the line $y=-x$.
steps: For $y=-x$ the coordinates swap and both change sign: $(x,y)\to(-y,-x)$.
Here $x=3$ and $y=-2$, so $-y=2$ and $-x=-3$.
Check: the midpoint of $(3,-2)$ and $(2,-3)$ is $(2.5,-2.5)$, which lies on $y=-x$.

misconceptions: Reflection in $y=-x$ is not the same as reflection in $y=x$. The second only swaps the coordinates; the first also flips both signs.
A reflected figure cannot be obtained by rotating the original. If an option is the original turned over, it is a mirror image, not a rotation.
Reflecting in the x-axis changes the sign of $y$, not of $x$. The axis named is the one whose points stay fixed.

recall.q: Where does $(x,y)$ go when reflected in the line $y=x$?
recall.a: To $(y,x)$.

recall.q: Where does $(x,y)$ go when reflected in the y-axis?
Which points stay fixed under a reflection?
recall.a: Exactly the points on the mirror line.

practice.stem: The point $(-3,5)$ is reflected in the line $y=-x$. What is its image?
practice.explanation: Across $y=-x$, $(x,y)$ goes to $(-y,-x)$, so $(-3,5)$ goes to $(-5,3)$. The option $(5,-3)$ tempts because it is the image across $y=x$, where only the swap happens. $(-3,-5)$ is the x-axis image and $(3,5)$ the y-axis image.

lesson.summary: Pick the mirror line, apply its coordinate rule, and verify that the midpoint of the point and its image lies on the line. A reflection reverses orientation, so no rotation can reproduce it.

topics.title: Rotation by 90°, 180° and 270°
points: About the origin: 90° anticlockwise (x, y) → (−y, x); 90° clockwise (x, y) → (y, −x); 180° (x, y) → (−x, −y), the same in both directions.
A rotation by θ clockwise equals one by 360° − θ anticlockwise, so 270° clockwise is 90° anticlockwise. Reduce any chain of turns to one net angle mod 360° before drawing.
On a clock face each hour mark is 30°, so a pointer at 12 turned 225° clockwise points at 225/30 = 7.5, the 7:30 position.
For a complicated figure, track one asymmetric feature such as a dot or an arrowhead and reject every option where that feature sits in the wrong place.
A rotation preserves orientation: a letter F rotated stays readable as an F at a slant, never a backwards F.

lesson.why: Rotation questions reduce to one turn about a point, and a wrong direction or a mis-added angle sends you to the wrong option.
lesson.intro: A rotation turns a figure about a fixed point, called the centre, without stretching or flipping it. Every point keeps its distance from the centre. Two things fix the turn: the angle and the direction, clockwise or anticlockwise. Several turns about the same centre in a row are the same as one turn whose angle is their sum.

definitions.meaning: The one point that stays where it is while everything else turns around it.
The single turn equal to a chain of turns: add the signed angles and reduce modulo 360°.

principle.text: About the origin, 90° anticlockwise sends $(x,y)$ to $(-y,x)$, 180° sends it to $(-x,-y)$, and 90° clockwise sends it to $(y,-x)$. A turn by $\theta$ clockwise equals a turn by $360^\circ-\theta$ anticlockwise.

lesson.limits: These formulas assume the centre is the origin and the y axis points up. For another centre, shift it to the origin, turn, and shift back. In a picture drawn with y pointing down, clockwise on the page flips the sign, so trust the picture over the formula.

example.problem: The point $(3,1)$ is turned 90° anticlockwise three times about the origin. Where does it end up?
steps: Three turns of 90° anticlockwise make a net turn of 270° anticlockwise, which is 90° clockwise.
90° clockwise sends $(x,y)$ to $(y,-x)$, so $(3,1)$ goes to $(1,-3)$.
Check by turning one step at a time: $(3,1)\to(-1,3)\to(-3,-1)\to(1,-3)$.

misconceptions: A rotation never mirrors a figure. A rotated letter F is still an F at a slant; a backwards F can only come from a reflection.
Turning a plate can change which letter it looks like: M turned 180° looks like W, and 6 looks like 9. Read the stem to see whether turned plates count as the same letter.

Only some capitals survive a 180° turn unchanged: H, I, N, O, S, X and Z. Others change (M becomes W, b becomes q) or become a non-letter. A stem that lets plates rotate may still treat a turned A or R as that same letter, so read its convention first.

A palindrome needs its letters in matched pairs. A word of odd length has exactly one letter left over, which sits in the middle, so five letters qualify only when exactly one letter occurs an odd number of times and the rest occur an even number of times. Three or more unpaired letters can never be arranged into a palindrome.
270° clockwise is not 270° anticlockwise. The two differ by a half turn, and 270° clockwise equals 90° anticlockwise.

recall.q: Where does $(x,y)$ go under a 90° anticlockwise turn about the origin?
Which single turn equals 270° clockwise?
recall.a: A turn of 90° anticlockwise.

recall.q: Does a rotation change a figure's handedness?
recall.a: No. A rotation keeps orientation, so a mirror image never comes from a rotation alone.

recall.q: What letter counts allow a five-letter palindrome?
recall.a: Exactly one letter occurs an odd number of times and every other letter an even number of times; the odd one goes in the middle.

practice.stem: The point $(2,5)$ is rotated 270° clockwise about the origin. Where does it land?
practice.explanation: 270° clockwise equals 90° anticlockwise, which sends $(x,y)$ to $(-y,x)$, giving $(-5,2)$. The option $(5,-2)$ tempts because it is the 90° clockwise result, the right formula for the wrong direction. $(-2,-5)$ is the 180° result.

lesson.summary: Reduce a chain of turns to one net angle, fix the direction, and apply the matching coordinate rule. A rotation never mirrors a figure.

topics.title: Translation and scaling
points: A translation by (a, b) sends (x, y) to (x + a, y + b): every point moves by the same vector, so shape, size and orientation are unchanged.
Scaling by factor k about a centre c sends P to c + k(P − c). With the origin as centre, (x, y) → (kx, ky). The centre is the only fixed point, and k = −1 is the point reflection in c.
Under scaling by k, lengths and perimeters multiply by k, areas by k² and volumes by k³; translation changes none of them.
Scaling with different factors on the two axes, (x, y) → (ax, by), multiplies area by ab and turns a circle into an ellipse, so the shape is no longer similar.

Scalings about one centre multiply their factors, and a translation commutes with scaling only when it is the zero vector, so scale-then-translate and translate-then-scale send a vertex to different places but give the same area.

lesson.why: Questions on translation and scaling ask for new coordinates or for how length, area and volume change. Mixing up the factors k, k squared and k cubed is the usual loss.
lesson.intro: A translation slides every point of a figure by the same step, so the shape, size and direction stay as they were. A scaling stretches or shrinks the figure from a fixed point, the centre, by one factor. A factor of 2 makes every length twice as long. Both moves can be written as a rule on the coordinates $(x,y)$.

definitions.meaning: The pair $(a,b)$ added to every point's coordinates.
The number $k$ that multiplies every length measured from the centre.
Figures with the same shape but possibly different size; scaling by one factor gives similar figures.

principle.text: A translation sends $(x,y)$ to $(x+a,y+b)$. Scaling about the origin by $k$ sends $(x,y)$ to $(kx,ky)$. Lengths multiply by $k$, areas by $k^2$ and volumes by $k^3$. Translation changes none of these.

lesson.limits: The area rule needs the same factor in every direction. If the x and y factors differ, $(x,y)\to(px,qy)$, the area multiplies by $pq$ and a circle becomes an ellipse. Scaling about a centre other than the origin first needs $P'=c+k(P-c)$.

example.problem: The triangle with corners $(1,1)$, $(5,1)$ and $(1,4)$ is scaled by 3 about the origin and then translated by $(2,-1)$. Find the new corners and the new area.
steps: The original base is 4 and height is 3, so its area is 6. Scaling by 3 multiplies it by 9, and the translation leaves it alone.
example.result: The corners are $(5,2)$, $(17,2)$, $(5,11)$ and the area is 54.

misconceptions: Doubling the sides does not double the area; it multiplies the area by 4 and a volume by 8.
Translating after scaling and scaling after translating give different positions. Apply the steps in the order stated.
A translation never changes area, so adding a vector to a scaled figure leaves its area at $k^2A$.

recall.q: By what factor does the area change when every length is scaled by $k$?
By what factor does the volume change under scaling by $k$?
What does a translation change about a figure?
recall.a: Only its position. Shape, size and orientation are unchanged.

practice.stem: A region of area 12 is scaled by 3 about a point and then translated by $(5,5)$. What is the area of the resulting region?
practice.explanation: Scaling by 3 multiplies the area by $3^2=9$, so the area becomes $12\times9=108$. The translation does not change area. The value 36 tempts because it multiplies the area by 3 instead of 9.

lesson.summary: Translation moves, scaling resizes about a centre. Lengths follow $k$, areas $k^2$, volumes $k^3$, and translation changes none of them.

topics.title: Line symmetry and rotational symmetry
points: A line of symmetry splits a figure into two mirror halves. A figure has rotational symmetry of order n when n different rotations in 0° ≤ θ < 360° map it onto itself, the smallest being 360°/n.
A regular n-gon has n lines of symmetry and rotational order n. A square has 4 and 4; a rectangle that is not a square has 2 and 2; a circle has infinitely many.
Line symmetry and rotational symmetry are independent: S, N, Z and a general parallelogram have order 2 but no line of symmetry, while A, T and an isosceles triangle have one line and order 1.
Capital letters with a vertical line of symmetry: A H I M O T U V W X Y. With a horizontal line: B C D E H I K O X. H, I, O and X have both.

lesson.why: Symmetry questions ask you to count lines, give an order, or find missing squares, and each is quickest once every part is paired with its mirror partner.
lesson.intro: A figure has line symmetry when a mirror line splits it into two halves that are reflections of each other. It has rotational symmetry when turning it by less than a full circle puts it exactly back onto itself. The number of different turns that do this, counting the turn by zero, is the order of rotational symmetry.

definitions.meaning: A line such that reflecting the figure in it gives back the same figure.
The number of turns in 0° ≤ θ < 360° that map the figure onto itself.

principle.text: A line is a line of symmetry when every part has an equal partner at the same distance on the other side of it. A figure of order $n$ maps onto itself under turns of $360^\circ/n$ and its multiples. A regular $n$-gon has $n$ lines and order $n$.

lesson.limits: The two kinds are independent. The letter S has order 2 but no line of symmetry, and an isosceles triangle has one line but order 1. Having one kind tells you nothing about the other.

example.problem: Find the lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry of a rectangle 4 units wide and 2 units tall.
steps: The vertical line through the middle swaps the left and right ends, and the horizontal line through the middle swaps top and bottom, so both are lines of symmetry.
A diagonal is not: reflecting in it would send the long side onto the short side, and their lengths differ.
A half turn about the centre sends each corner to the opposite corner, so it maps the rectangle onto itself. A quarter turn would give a 2 by 4 rectangle, which is a different position.
example.result: 2 lines of symmetry and rotational order 2, from the turns 0° and 180°.

misconceptions: The diagonals of a rectangle are not lines of symmetry. Among parallelograms, only a rhombus (and so a square) has diagonals that are lines of symmetry.
A shape with rotational symmetry need not have a line of symmetry. S, N, Z and a general parallelogram all have order 2 and no line.
Symmetry and convexity are separate tests. A polygon is convex only if no segment between two of its points leaves it, so a notch or inward corner makes it non-convex.

recall.q: What is a line of symmetry?
recall.a: A line that splits a figure into two halves that are mirror images of each other.

recall.q: How many lines of symmetry and what rotational order does a regular hexagon have?
recall.a: 6 lines and order 6.

recall.q: How do you find the squares to add so a line becomes a line of symmetry?
recall.a: Look at each filled square's mirror partner across the line, in the same row or column, and add every partner that is empty.

recall.q: What shows that a polygon is not convex?
recall.a: Two of its points whose joining segment leaves the shape, which an inward notch or corner causes.

practice.stem: A vertical mirror line runs between column $-1$ and column $0$ of a grid. The filled squares, as (row, column), are $(0,-1)$, $(1,-2)$, $(1,-1)$ and $(0,0)$. What is the least number of squares to add so the line becomes a line of symmetry?
practice.explanation: The partner of the square at (row, $c$) is (row, $-1-c$). The squares $(0,-1)$ and $(0,0)$ already pair with each other. The square $(1,-2)$ needs $(1,1)$ and the square $(1,-1)$ needs $(1,0)$, and both are empty, so 2 squares are added. The answer 3 tempts if you count $(0,0)$ as unpaired, forgetting it is the partner of $(0,-1)$.

lesson.summary: Pair every part with its partner across the line, count the empty partners, and remember that line symmetry and rotational symmetry are independent of each other.

topics.title: Combining transformations
points: Apply composed transformations right to left as written, or in the order the question states; the order matters, since rotating then reflecting usually differs from reflecting then rotating.
Two reflections in lines meeting at angle α give a rotation by 2α about the meeting point. Two reflections in parallel lines a distance d apart give a translation by 2d.

An even number of reflections preserves orientation, an odd number reverses it. So rotate 90° clockwise and then reflect in y = x is a single reflection: (x, y) → (y, −x) → (−x, y), the reflection in the y-axis.
Rotation and scaling about the same centre commute; a translation and a rotation generally do not.

lesson.why: Questions show a figure before and after two operations and ask which operations did it, and swapping the order of the operations changes the result.
lesson.intro: A transformation moves every point of a figure by a fixed rule: a reflection flips it in a line, a rotation turns it about a point, and a translation slides it. Composing means doing one transformation and then another on the result. Doing A then B is generally not the same as doing B then A, so the order has to be kept.

definitions.meaning: Doing one transformation and then another on the result, read in the order the question states.
Whether a figure reads clockwise or anticlockwise; a reflection reverses it and a rotation or translation keeps it.

principle.text: Each reflection reverses orientation and each rotation or translation keeps it, so an even number of reflections preserves orientation and an odd number reverses it. Two reflections in lines meeting at angle $\alpha$ make a rotation by $2\alpha$; in parallel lines a distance $d$ apart they make a translation by $2d$.

lesson.limits: Order matters: rotating then reflecting usually differs from reflecting then rotating. A rotation and a scaling about the same centre do commute, but a translation and a rotation generally do not. When only the start and end figures are given, several pairs of operations can fit, so follow one marked feature to pick the pair the options name.

example.problem: The point $(4,1)$ is reflected in the x axis and then rotated 90° anticlockwise about the origin. Where does it land, and where if the order is swapped?
steps: Reflection in the x axis sends $(x,y)$ to $(x,-y)$, so $(4,1)$ goes to $(4,-1)$.
A 90° anticlockwise turn sends $(x,y)$ to $(-y,x)$, so $(4,-1)$ goes to $(1,4)$.
In the swapped order the turn comes first and gives $(-1,4)$, and the reflection then gives $(-1,-4)$.
example.result: $(1,4)$ in the stated order and $(-1,-4)$ when swapped, so the order matters.

misconceptions: In "reflect, then rotate" the reflection acts first. Apply the operations in the order the question states.
A reflection along a horizontal line swaps up and down, and one along a vertical line swaps left and right. Read the line, not the direction you imagine the flip going.
If an option shows a mirrored figure, an odd number of reflections was involved, and a rotation alone can never produce it.

recall.q: How does a chain of operations change orientation?
recall.a: Each reflection reverses it, so an even number of reflections preserves orientation and an odd number reverses it.

recall.q: What does a reflection in a horizontal line swap?
recall.a: Up and down; left and right stay as they were.

recall.q: What single transformation do two reflections in lines meeting at 40° make?
recall.a: A rotation by 80° about the point where the lines meet.

recall.q: What do two reflections in parallel lines a distance $d$ apart make?
recall.a: A translation by $2d$ perpendicular to the lines.

practice.stem: A figure is reflected in the x axis and then in a line through the origin at 30° to the x axis. This equals a single
practice.explanation: Two reflections in lines meeting at 30° make a rotation by $2\times30^\circ=60^\circ$ about the meeting point, here the origin. A single reflection would need an odd number of reflections, and a translation needs parallel lines. A rotation by 30° tempts because 30° is the angle between the lines, but the turn is twice that angle.

lesson.summary: Apply the operations in the stated order, count reflections to know whether orientation flips, and use the rule that two reflections make a rotation by twice the angle between the lines.

topics.title: Mirror images and water images
points: A mirror image (mirror standing to the side) reflects across a vertical axis: left and right swap, top and bottom stay.
A water image (lake below the object) reflects across a horizontal axis: top and bottom swap, left and right stay.
For a word in a mirror, the letter order reverses and each letter is flipped left to right, so WATER reads R-E-T-A-W with E and R reversed and W, A, T unchanged.

A word looks identical in a mirror only if it is a palindrome built from letters with a vertical line of symmetry (OTTO, WOW). A word looks identical in water when every letter has a horizontal line of symmetry (CODE, HIDE, BOX).
Applying a mirror image and then a water image to a figure gives a 180° rotation, not a reflection.

lesson.why: Mirror and water image questions turn on one fact: which direction the figure flips. Reversing the wrong way, or the wrong letters, picks the wrong option.
lesson.intro: A mirror image is what you see when a mirror stands beside the object: left and right swap, while top and bottom stay. A water image is what you see when the object stands above a lake: top and bottom swap, while left and right stay. For a word, a mirror also reverses the order of the letters, because the last letter now appears first. Each letter is flipped as well.

definitions.meaning: The upright line a mirror image is flipped across.
The level line a water image is flipped across.

principle.text: A mirror image flips left and right, so a word reverses its letter order and each letter is flipped left to right. A water image flips top and bottom, so the order stays and each letter is flipped upside down. A letter is unchanged by a flip only if it is symmetric about that axis.

lesson.limits: Letters symmetric about the vertical axis are A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y in capitals. Those symmetric about the horizontal axis are B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O, X. These lists apply to plain capitals; a stem that uses a different font or lower case needs the letters checked again.

example.problem: Does DECK look the same in a water image, and does TOOT look the same in a mirror?
steps: Water flips top and bottom. D, E, C and K are each symmetric about a horizontal line, and the order is unchanged, so DECK reads the same.
A mirror reverses the order and flips each letter left to right. TOOT reversed is TOOT.
T and O are each symmetric about a vertical line, so each letter looks unchanged as well.
example.result: Both words look unchanged: DECK in water, TOOT in a mirror.

misconceptions: A water image does not reverse the letter order. Only a mirror reverses the order.
A palindrome alone is not enough for a mirror: each letter must also be symmetric left to right, so TOOT works but BOB does not.
Mirror followed by water is not a reflection. Together they give a 180 degree rotation of the figure.

recall.q: Which direction does a water image flip?
recall.a: Top and bottom, across a horizontal axis. Left and right stay.

recall.q: What happens to the letter order of a word in a mirror?
recall.a: It reverses, and each letter is also flipped left to right.

recall.q: When does a word look unchanged in a water image?
recall.a: When every letter is symmetric about a horizontal line, as in CODE.

practice.stem: Which of these words looks exactly the same in its water image?
practice.explanation: Water flips top to bottom without reordering the letters. D, I, C and E are each symmetric about a horizontal line, so DICE is unchanged. TOWN tempts because T and O are symmetric, but both are symmetric about a vertical line and T is not about a horizontal one. L, P and S have no horizontal symmetry.

lesson.summary: Decide the axis first. A mirror reverses the order and flips letters left to right, while water keeps the order and flips letters upside down. Only symmetric letters survive a flip unchanged.

topics.title: Mirror images of clocks
points: A vertical mirror sends a hand at angle θ (clockwise from 12) to 360° − θ. Both hands obey this consistently, so the image always shows a valid time.
The actual time is 11:60 − the time seen in the mirror, and the rule works in both directions: if the mirror shows 4:20 the clock reads 7:40.
Times that look the same in a mirror are 12:00 and 6:00, where both hands lie on the vertical 12–6 line.

A water image of a clock sends θ to 180° − θ for each hand, which never gives a consistent clock face (the hour hand always sits 15° off where the minute hand puts it), so questions on clock images are almost always about mirrors.

lesson.why: A clock seen in a mirror is a short calculation if you know the rule, and a slow guess if you do not. It is a small but reliable source of marks.
lesson.intro: A clock face has its 12 at the top. In a mirror, left and right swap, so a hand that points 100 degrees clockwise from 12 now points 100 degrees anticlockwise from 12, which is 260 degrees clockwise. Both hands swap the same way, so the mirror always shows a valid time. That time is easy to find from the actual time and back again with one subtraction.

definitions.meaning: The time read from the reflected clock face.

principle.text: The actual time and the mirror time add up to 12:00. Written as 11:60 to avoid borrowing, the actual time is 11:60 minus the time shown.

lesson.limits: The rule is for a mirror standing to the side, which flips left and right. A water image flips top and bottom and does not give a consistent clock. The rule also assumes a normal 12-hour dial with the hands at the correct relative positions. If the subtraction gives a zero or negative hour, add 12 to the hour (12:10 in the mirror gives $11-12=-1$, so $-1+12=11$, and the clock reads 11:50); a result of 60 minutes rolls into the next hour.

example.problem: A clock seen in a mirror shows 4:20. What is the actual time?
steps: Subtract from 11:60: hours $11-4=7$ and minutes $60-20=40$.
So the actual time is 7:40.
Check with angles: at 7:40 the hour hand is at 230 degrees and the minute hand at 240 degrees. Their mirror angles are 130 and 120 degrees, which is where 4:20 puts them.

misconceptions: Subtracting hours and minutes separately from 12:00 invites a borrowing slip, such as 12 minus 4 hours and 60 minus 20 minutes giving 8:40. Using 11:60 avoids the borrow.
Reflecting only the minute hand, or only the hour hand, gives an inconsistent time. The rule moves both together.
The rule works in both directions: the mirror time is also 11:60 minus the actual time.

recall.q: What is the actual time if the mirror shows 4:20?
Which common times look the same in a mirror?
recall.a: 12:00 and 6:00, where both hands lie on the vertical line.

recall.q: Why do clock questions use a mirror and not water?
recall.a: A water image puts the hour hand in a position the minute hand does not support, so it is not a valid clock.

practice.stem: In a mirror a wall clock appears to show 9:15. What is the actual time?
practice.explanation: Actual time is 11:60 minus 9:15: hours $11-9=2$ and minutes $60-15=45$, so 2:45. The option 9:45 tempts because it only mirrors the minute hand, and 3:45 comes from borrowing the hour twice.

lesson.summary: For a mirror clock, subtract the shown time from 11:60. The same subtraction converts back, and 12:00 and 6:00 are their own mirror images.

topics.title: Painted cubes and cuboids cut into unit cubes
points: An n × n × n cube painted outside and cut into n³ unit cubes has 8 corner cubes (3 faces painted), 12(n − 2) edge cubes (2 faces), 6(n − 2)² face cubes (1 face) and (n − 2)³ hidden cubes (0 faces), for n ≥ 2.
The four counts add up to n³: for n = 4 they are 8 + 24 + 24 + 8 = 64. Checking the sum catches most slips.
For an a × b × c cuboid with every side ≥ 2: 8 corners, 4[(a−2)+(b−2)+(c−2)] two-face cubes, 2[(a−2)(b−2)+(b−2)(c−2)+(c−2)(a−2)] one-face cubes and (a−2)(b−2)(c−2) unpainted ones.
Cutting a block with p, q and r cuts parallel to the three face pairs gives (p + 1)(q + 1)(r + 1) pieces, so n³ equal cubes need 3(n − 1) cuts when pieces are not restacked.
If only some faces are painted (for example all except the bottom), recount by position instead of reusing the formulas: the bottom layer's corners then have only 2 painted faces.

lesson.why: Painted cube questions are short counting problems, and the formulas are easy to misuse with n instead of n minus 2. They appear as 1-mark NAT questions.
lesson.intro: Paint the outside of a big cube, then cut it into small unit cubes. A small cube is painted only on the faces that were on the outside. Cubes at a corner of the big cube touch three outside faces. Cubes along an edge touch two, cubes in the middle of a face touch one, and cubes buried inside touch none. Counting each kind by position gives the answer.

definitions.meaning: A unit cube at a corner; three faces painted.
A unit cube on an edge but not a corner; two faces painted.
A unit cube in the interior of a face; one face painted.
A unit cube with no outside face; no paint.

principle.text: For an $a\times b\times c$ block painted on all sides, with every side at least 2, there are 8 corner cubes, $4[(a-2)+(b-2)+(c-2)]$ edge cubes, $2[(a-2)(b-2)+(b-2)(c-2)+(c-2)(a-2)]$ face cubes and $(a-2)(b-2)(c-2)$ core cubes. For an $n\times n\times n$ cube these are $8$, $12(n-2)$, $6(n-2)^2$ and $(n-2)^3$.

lesson.limits: These counts assume all six faces are painted and every side is at least 2. If one face is left unpainted, count by position instead: the cubes along that face lose one painted side. For a side of 1 the formulas break down.

example.problem: A cube with sides of 5 units, painted on every face, is cut into 125 unit cubes. How many have exactly two painted faces, and how many have exactly one?
steps: Here $n=5$, so $n-2=3$.
Edge cubes: a cube has 12 edges, each with 3 non-corner cubes, giving $12\times3=36$.
Face cubes: 6 faces, each with a $3\times3$ interior, giving $6\times9=54$.
Check: the corners and core add $8+27=35$, and $36+54+35=125$.
example.result: 36 cubes have two painted faces and 54 have one.

misconceptions: The edge count uses $n-2$, not $n$: the two end cubes of each edge are corners and are counted separately.
The all-faces formulas cannot be reused when a face is unpainted. Recount layer by layer.
Always check that the four counts add to $a\times b\times c$. A sum that is off points to a slip in one of the terms.

recall.q: How many corner cubes does a painted cuboid have?
recall.a: Always 8, when every side is at least 2.

recall.q: How many cubes of an $n\times n\times n$ block have no paint?
recall.a: $(n-2)^3$, the cubes strictly inside.

recall.q: Why is $n-2$ used for edges and faces?
recall.a: The two end cubes on each edge belong to corners, so only $n-2$ remain.

practice.stem: A $3\times4\times6$ cuboid is painted on all six faces and cut into unit cubes. How many unit cubes have exactly one painted face?
practice.explanation: With $a-2=1$, $b-2=2$, $c-2=4$, the face cubes number $2[1\cdot2+2\cdot4+4\cdot1]=2\times14=28$. The value 8 tempts because it is the corner count. Check: corners 8, edge cubes $4(1+2+4)=28$, face cubes 28 and core cubes $1\cdot2\cdot4=8$ add to 72, the volume.

lesson.summary: Classify unit cubes by position, use sides minus 2 for the interior counts, and check that the four counts sum to the volume.

topics.title: Faces, edges and vertices of polyhedra
points: Euler's formula for any convex polyhedron: V − E + F = 2. A cube has V = 8, E = 12, F = 6 and 8 − 12 + 6 = 2.
Count edges from the faces: every edge borders exactly two faces, so 2E = total number of sides of all faces. Count vertices the same way: 2E = sum of the degrees of the vertices.
Platonic solids (V, E, F): tetrahedron (4, 6, 4), cube (8, 12, 6), octahedron (6, 12, 8), dodecahedron (20, 30, 12), icosahedron (12, 30, 20).
A prism on an n-gon has 2n vertices, 3n edges and n + 2 faces; a pyramid on an n-gon has n + 1 vertices, 2n edges and n + 1 faces.

lesson.why: Face, edge and vertex counts feed straight into Euler's formula, and the same habit of counting parts helps with questions about cutting a solid into pieces.
lesson.intro: A polyhedron is a solid whose surface is made of flat polygons. The polygons are its faces, the segments where two faces meet are its edges, and the points where edges meet are its vertices. For a cube these counts are 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

definitions.meaning: The number $V-E+F$, which equals 2 for every convex polyhedron.

principle.text: For a convex polyhedron with $V$ vertices, $E$ edges and $F$ faces, $V-E+F=2$. Each edge borders exactly two faces, so the sides of all the faces add up to $2E$.

lesson.limits: The formula holds for convex solids and for any solid without holes. A solid with one hole through it, such as a picture frame, gives $V-E+F=0$. The formula says nothing about cuts: each full straight cut splits a piece into at most two, so $k$ cuts give at most $2^k$ pieces.

example.problem: A hexagonal prism has two hexagonal faces and six rectangular faces. Find its numbers of edges and vertices.
steps: Add the sides of all the faces: $2\times6+6\times4=36$.
Each edge borders two faces, so it is counted twice, and $E=36/2=18$.
There are $F=2+6=8$ faces, and $V-E+F=2$ gives $V=2+18-8=12$.
example.result: The prism has $E=18$ edges and $V=12$ vertices.

misconceptions: Adding the sides of the faces gives $2E$, not $E$. Forgetting to halve doubles the edge count.
Euler's formula links three counts, so it needs two of them before it gives the third; it cannot find edges from faces alone.

recall.q: State Euler's formula for a convex polyhedron.
How do you get the number of edges from the faces?
recall.a: Add the sides of all the faces and halve the total, because each edge borders two faces.

recall.q: Why can two full straight cuts never give 8 pieces?
recall.a: Each cut at most doubles the number of pieces, so two cuts give at most $2^2=4$.

recall.q: What does $V-E+F$ equal for a solid with one hole through it?
recall.a: 0, not 2.

practice.stem: A polyhedron has 8 triangular faces and 6 square faces and no holes. How many vertices does it have?
practice.explanation: The sides of all faces total $8\times3+6\times4=48$, so $E=24$. There are $F=14$ faces, and $V=2+E-F=12$. The number 14 tempts if you stop at the face count, and 48 if you forget to halve.

lesson.summary: Halve the total of the faces' sides to get the edges, then use $V-E+F=2$ for the missing count. For cuts, remember that $k$ full cuts give at most $2^k$ pieces.

topics.title: Cube nets: which faces end up opposite
points: A net is a flat arrangement of 6 edge-joined squares that folds into a cube. Exactly 11 distinct nets exist; a 2 × 3 block, a row of 5 or more, and any shape with 4 squares round one corner do not fold.
In any straight run of squares, alternate squares are opposite: in a row of four, the 1st and 3rd and the 2nd and 4th become opposite faces.
In a zigzag of four squares (a Z or S shape), the two end squares are opposite.
Two squares that share an edge or even just a corner point in the net share a vertex of the cube, so they can never be opposite. Use this to strike out options fast.
To check a proposed folded cube, find its three visible faces, confirm no two of them are opposite in the net, and then check their cyclic order around the shared corner.

lesson.why: Net questions ask which faces touch on the folded cube, and the answer comes from knowing which pairs of faces are opposite.
lesson.intro: A net is a flat pattern of six squares, joined edge to edge, that folds into a cube. Each square becomes one face. Two faces of the cube are opposite when they never touch, and every face has exactly one opposite, so the faces form three opposite pairs. A picture of the folded cube shows at most three faces from one corner, and these can never include an opposite pair.

definitions.meaning: Two faces of a cube that share no edge; each face has exactly one.
A flat arrangement of six edge-joined squares that folds into a cube.

principle.text: In a straight run of squares, squares two places apart are opposite: in a row of four, the 1st and 3rd and the 2nd and 4th are opposite pairs. In a zigzag of four squares, the two end squares are opposite. Squares that share an edge in the net touch on the cube, so they are never opposite.

lesson.limits: The run rule needs squares in one straight line, joined edge to edge. Opposite pairs do not tell you the order in which three faces go around a corner; for that, fold the net square by square. Only 11 arrangements of six squares fold into a cube, and a row of five or a 2 by 3 block does not.

example.problem: Squares 1, 2, 3 and 4 form a row. Square 5 sits above square 2 and square 6 sits below square 4. Which faces are opposite on the folded cube?
steps: In the row of four, the 1st and 3rd squares are opposite and the 2nd and 4th are opposite, giving the pairs 1-3 and 2-4.
Squares 5 and 6 are the only ones left, so they form the third pair.
Neither pair breaks the edge rule: 5 touches only square 2 and 6 touches only square 4, so neither is opposite its neighbour.

misconceptions: Squares far apart in the flat net can still touch on the cube. Distance on paper does not decide which faces are opposite; the run and zigzag rules do.
A cube picture is not right just because it shows the correct symbols. If it shows two opposite faces side by side, it is wrong, so check the visible faces against the pairs.

recall.q: How many opposite pairs does a cube have?
recall.a: Three, because every face has exactly one opposite.

recall.q: Which squares are opposite in a row of four in a net?
recall.a: The 1st and 3rd, and the 2nd and 4th.

recall.q: Can two squares that share an edge in a net be opposite?
recall.a: No. They meet along that edge on the folded cube.

recall.q: How do you quickly reject a picture of a folded cube?
recall.a: Find an opposite pair among its visible faces; a view from one corner never shows two opposite faces.

practice.stem: A net has squares 1, 2, 3 in a row. Square 4 sits above square 1. Square 5 sits below square 3, and square 6 sits to the right of square 5. Which two faces are opposite on the folded cube?
practice.explanation: The row of three makes 1 and 3 opposite, and rolling a cube over the net gives the other pairs 4-5 and 2-6. The pairs 1 and 2, and 3 and 5, share an edge in the net, so they cannot be opposite. The pair 4 and 6 tempts because they sit farthest apart on paper, but distance in the flat pattern does not decide it.

lesson.summary: Find the opposite pairs from straight runs and zigzags, never pair squares that share an edge, and reject any folded-cube picture that shows an opposite pair together.

topics.title: Dice: opposite faces from several views
points: Each view of a die shows three mutually adjacent faces meeting at one corner. Every number visible together with X is a neighbour of X, so once four neighbours of X are known the sixth number is opposite X.

One common face: list each view clockwise starting from the common face. Numbers in matching positions are opposite: views (3, 1, 2) and (3, 4, 5) give 1 opposite 4 and 2 opposite 5, and the remaining sixth number is opposite 3.
Two common faces a and b: the views are the two corners at the ends of edge a–b, read clockwise as (a, b, x) and (b, a, y), so x is opposite y.
A standard die has opposite faces summing to 7 (1–6, 2–5, 3–4), so on a standard die 3 and 4 can never be seen together.
Rolling a die one step tips it over an edge: the face that was on top goes to the side it rolled towards. Four rolls in the same direction bring it back to the start.

lesson.why: Dice questions ask which number sits opposite another when several views are shown. A systematic method beats guessing, and the same method works on every variant.
lesson.intro: A die has six faces, and from any one viewpoint you see three of them, all meeting at one corner. Any two faces seen together are neighbours, never opposites. Every time a number appears next to another across several views, you learn one neighbour. A face has four neighbours and one opposite, so once four neighbours are known, the opposite is the sixth number.

definitions.meaning: A face that appears in more than one view.
A die whose opposite faces add to 7: 1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4.

principle.text: If two views share one face, list each view clockwise starting from that common face. Numbers in matching positions are opposite. The remaining sixth number is opposite the common face.

lesson.limits: The sum-7 rule holds only when the question says the die is standard. The matching-position method needs both views listed in the same rotational direction. Views of the same two faces from the two ends of a shared edge (two common faces) follow a different pairing.

example.problem: One view of a die shows 2, 1, 4 clockwise from the top face 2. Another view shows 2, 6, 3 clockwise from the same face 2. Which numbers are opposite which?
steps: List both views clockwise starting from 2: first view (2, 1, 4), second view (2, 6, 3).
Pair matching positions: 1 with 6, and 4 with 3.
The neighbours of 2 are 1, 4, 6 and 3, so the number left over, 5, is opposite 2.
example.result: 1 is opposite 6, 4 is opposite 3, and 5 is opposite 2.

misconceptions: Two numbers visible in the same view are always adjacent, never opposite.
Do not use the sum-7 rule unless the die is stated to be standard.
Reading one view clockwise and the other anticlockwise swaps the pairs and gives wrong opposites.

recall.q: How many faces of a die can you see in one view?
recall.a: Three, all meeting at one corner and all adjacent to each other.

recall.q: With four known neighbours of a face, how do you find its opposite?
recall.a: It is the one number not among the four neighbours and not the face itself.

recall.q: When may you use the rule that opposite faces sum to 7?
recall.a: Only when the die is stated to be standard.

practice.stem: A die is shown in two views, both listed clockwise from the common face 5: (5, 2, 3) and (5, 6, 1). Which number is opposite 3?
practice.explanation: Matching positions give 2 opposite 6 and 3 opposite 1, which leaves 4 opposite 5. So 3 is opposite 1. The option 6 tempts because it is opposite 2, the neighbour listed beside 3, and 4 is opposite the common face 5.

lesson.summary: Find a common face, read both views clockwise from it, and pair matching positions. The leftover number is opposite the common face.

topics.title: Paper folding, punching and cutting
points: Each fold doubles the number of layers, so k folds of a sheet give 2^k layers and a hole punched through all of them away from any crease becomes 2^k holes.
Unfold in reverse order, one fold at a time: at each step draw the mirror image of every hole and cut across that fold line, then unfold the next.

A hole punched on a folded edge cuts through the U-bends of that crease, so each bend gives one hole centred on the crease instead of two. After k folds, a hole on the last crease gives 2^(k−1) holes.
The opened pattern is symmetric about the first crease, which spans the whole sheet; each later crease is a mirror only for the panels it joins, so test symmetry panel by panel.
A cut along a fold line separates the sheet into pieces rather than making a hole; count pieces by tracing which layers the cut actually passes through.
A strip folded in half k times and cut once straight across all layers, away from the creases, falls into 2^k + 1 pieces: the cut becomes 2^k parallel cuts in the opened strip.

lesson.why: Fold-and-punch questions are answered by unfolding in reverse order, and counting layers tells you how many holes or pieces to expect.
lesson.intro: Folding a sheet lays one part of it flat on another, so each fold doubles the number of layers. A punch or cut made through the folded sheet goes through every layer at once. When the sheet is opened, each layer carries its own copy of the mark. The copies are mirror images of one another across the creases.

definitions.meaning: The line along which the sheet was folded.
One thickness of paper in the folded sheet; a punch makes a mark in every layer.

principle.text: After $k$ folds there are $2^k$ layers, so a mark away from every crease appears $2^k$ times. To open the sheet, undo the folds in reverse order and at each step add the mirror image of every mark across that crease. When the stem says each fold is made along the line of symmetry perpendicular to the long edge, each fold halves one side only, so keep the pair of side lengths and halve the longer side at every fold; the perimeter is $2(a+b)$ of the final pair.

lesson.limits: A mark that touches a crease joins its own mirror image into one larger mark instead of making a separate copy, so the count is lower: a hole centred on the last crease gives $2^{k-1}$ holes. A cut along a crease separates the sheet rather than making a hole. Where a sheet is transparent every layer shows, and an opaque one hides the lower layers.

example.problem: A unit square sheet is folded in half along the line $x=0.5$ and then in half along $y=0.5$. A round hole is punched at $(0.2,0.3)$ of the folded sheet. Where are the holes on the opened sheet?
steps: Two folds give $2^2=4$ layers, and the hole is away from both creases, so there are 4 holes.
Undo the last fold, along $y=0.5$: the mirror of $(0.2,0.3)$ is $(0.2,0.7)$.
Undo the first fold, along $x=0.5$: the mirrors of both holes are $(0.8,0.3)$ and $(0.8,0.7)$.

misconceptions: Unfold in the reverse of the folding order. The last fold made is the first one undone, and the mirror image must be taken across that crease.
A hole on a crease merges with its mirror image into one larger hole. A square touching a horizontal crease unfolds into a rectangle twice as tall, not into two squares.

After each fold of a rectangle, compare the sides again before the next fold, because the side the next crease crosses can change. A $24\times10$ sheet folded three times goes $24\times10$, $12\times10$, $6\times10$, then $6\times5$, since 10 has become the longer side; the perimeter is $2(6+5)=22$. Halving 24 three times would wrongly give $3\times10$.

recall.q: How many layers do $k$ folds make?
recall.a: $2^k$ layers.

recall.q: In what order do you unfold a sheet?
recall.a: In reverse: undo the last fold first, mirroring every mark across that crease.

recall.q: What happens to a mark that touches a crease when the sheet is opened?
recall.a: It joins its mirror image into one larger mark across the crease.

recall.q: A $12\times5$ sheet is folded once along the line that halves its long side. What are the new sides?
recall.a: $6\times5$.

practice.stem: A long strip of paper is folded in half three times, each time along the middle of the folded strip. One straight cut is then made across all the layers, away from every crease. Into how many pieces does the strip fall?
practice.explanation: Three folds make $2^3=8$ layers, so the cut becomes 8 parallel cuts across the opened strip. Eight cuts across a strip leave $8+1=9$ pieces. The answer 8 tempts if you count layers instead of pieces.

lesson.summary: Count layers as $2^k$, unfold in reverse order mirroring every mark across each crease, and treat marks on a crease as merging with their mirror images.

topics.title: Crease patterns
points: Folding a strip in half k times in the same direction and unfolding leaves 2^k − 1 parallel creases dividing it into 2^k equal panels.

Folding a square in half along one centre line and then along the other leaves two perpendicular creases through the centre, dividing it into 4 equal squares; folding that quarter along its diagonal through the centre adds both diagonals of the original square, giving 8 congruent triangles.
Every new crease is reflected through all earlier creases when the sheet is opened, so each fold adds twice as many crease segments as the one before.
Folds need not be halves: a letter fold into thirds makes 3 layers, 2 creases and 3 panels. Count panels as layers, and creases as panels minus one for parallel folds.

lesson.why: Crease questions ask how many fold lines or equal panels appear once a folded sheet is opened, and the answer comes from a short counting rule instead of drawing every fold.
lesson.intro: A crease is the line left in paper where it was folded and then opened out again. Fold a strip in half and open it, and one crease sits in the middle. Fold it in half twice in the same direction and open it, and the first fold has been folded again, so it is still there, and the second fold has added a crease in the middle of each half. The creases cut the strip into equal pieces, and the whole question is how many creases and pieces there are.

definitions.meaning: The line left in the paper by a fold after the sheet is opened out again.
One flat piece of the opened sheet between neighbouring creases.
One thickness of paper in the folded sheet.

principle.text: Folding a strip in half $k$ times in the same direction gives $2^k$ layers. Opened out, it has $2^k$ equal panels and $2^k-1$ creases. For any parallel folds, the creases number one fewer than the panels. Each new fold adds one new crease in every panel that already exists, so the number added doubles at every fold.

lesson.limits: The rule needs every fold to be a half-fold made the same way on the whole stack. A fold into thirds gives 3 panels and 2 creases instead. On a square, folds along different directions cross, so the strip count does not apply: count the lines and the regions they cut separately.

example.problem: A strip of paper 40 cm long is folded in half three times in the same direction, then opened out completely. How many creases are there, and how wide is each panel?
steps: Three half-folds make $2^3=8$ layers, so the opened strip has 8 equal panels.
The creases are one fewer than the panels: $8-1=7$. Check by adding what each fold contributes: $1+2+4=7$.
The panels share the 40 cm equally, so each is $40/8=5$ cm wide.
example.result: 7 creases and 8 panels, each 5 cm wide.

misconceptions: Counting creases as $2^k$. The number of panels is $2^k$, and creases lie between panels, so there is one fewer: $2^k-1$.
Thinking the second fold removes the first crease. Opening the sheet leaves every earlier crease in place, and each later fold adds new ones between them.
Applying the strip rule to thirds. A letter fold makes 3 panels and 2 creases, not 4 and 3.

recall.q: How many creases does a strip folded in half $k$ times in the same direction have when opened?
recall.a: $2^k-1$ creases, dividing it into $2^k$ equal panels.

recall.q: For parallel folds, how are the number of creases and panels related?
recall.a: There is one crease fewer than panels, because creases lie between panels.

recall.q: A square is folded in half along one centre line, then the other, then its quarter along the diagonal. How many congruent triangles does the opened square show?
recall.a: Eight, cut out by the two centre lines and the two diagonals.

practice.stem: A long strip of paper is folded in half five times in the same direction and then opened out completely. How many creases does it show?
practice.explanation: Five half-folds give $2^5=32$ panels, and the creases are one fewer than the panels, so $32-1=31$. The answer 32 tempts if you count panels instead of the lines between them.

lesson.summary: Parallel half-folds give $2^k$ panels and $2^k-1$ creases, every fold keeps the earlier creases, and a fold into thirds or a fold in a second direction needs its own count.

topics.title: Assembling pieces and grouping figures
points: To decide whether pieces assemble into a target, first check invariants: total area must match, piece shapes must match up to the allowed moves, and colour counts must match any colouring argument.

Chessboard colouring settles many tiling questions: each domino covers one dark and one light square, so an 8 × 8 board with two opposite corners removed (30 of one colour, 32 of the other) cannot be tiled by 31 dominoes.
Pieces may be rotated freely; turning a piece over is a reflection and is allowed only if the question says so. An L-shaped piece and its mirror image are different pieces in a flat puzzle.
Grouping questions ask which figures belong together under a transformation: group shapes that are rotations of one another and separate their mirror images.

To group or find the odd one out, turn each figure until one chosen feature (a dot, the longest arm) points the same way, then compare: figures that match are rotations of each other, and one that matches only after turning over is a mirror image.
Counting figures in a grid: an n × n grid of unit squares holds 1² + 2² + … + n² squares and C(n + 1, 2)² rectangles, so a 4 × 4 grid has 30 squares and 100 rectangles.

lesson.why: Assembly questions ask whether given pieces can make a target shape or how pieces must be cut, and a quick count of cells usually settles them before any drawing is tried.
lesson.intro: A piece is a group of unit squares joined edge to edge. To build a target from pieces, the pieces must cover the target exactly, with no gap and no overlap. Pieces can be turned, but not resized, so each piece covers a fixed number of squares. That gives the first test: count the squares in the target and compare with what the pieces can add up to. When the counts agree, colour the squares like a chessboard and count each colour, since a piece may cover its colours unevenly.

definitions.meaning: Covering a shape completely with pieces that do not overlap and leave no gap.
Colouring the squares in two alternating colours and showing that the pieces cannot cover the two colours in the counts the target has.
A piece flipped over, like an L and its reverse. It cannot be turned into the original by rotation alone.

principle.text: A target can be built only if its square count is a sum of the piece sizes. If every piece has $k$ squares, the count must be a multiple of $k$. A domino covers one dark and one light square, so a target tileable by dominoes has equally many of each colour.
principle.tex: N_{\text{target}}=\sum_i n_i\,s_i,\qquad n_i\ge 0,\ s_i=\text{squares in piece } i

lesson.limits: These tests only rule shapes out. A target that passes the count and colour tests may still fail to tile, so confirm a buildable answer by actually placing the pieces. When a square is cut into two parts and one part is given, the other part is the square minus the given cells, and it must have exactly that outline. Similar-shape questions allow scaling, so for them compare angles and side ratios, not square counts.

example.problem: A $6\times 6$ board has two opposite corner squares removed. Can the remaining squares be covered by 17 dominoes, each covering two edge-adjacent squares?
steps: The board has $36-2=34$ squares, and 17 dominoes cover $17\times 2=34$, so the count test passes.
Colour the board like a chessboard. Opposite corners have the same colour, so both removed squares are of one colour, leaving 16 squares of that colour and 18 of the other.
Each domino covers one square of each colour, so 17 dominoes cover 17 of each colour. The board has 16 and 18, which does not match.
example.result: No. The counts are equal in total but unequal by colour, so the tiling is impossible.

misconceptions: A matching square count does not prove a tiling exists. Count first to reject, then place the pieces to confirm.
A mirror image is not the same piece. Rotating is always allowed, but flipping a piece over is allowed only if the question says so, so an L and its reverse are different pieces.
To find the missing part of a cut square, people compare options with the given piece. Subtract the given piece's cells from the whole square instead, then match the outline of what is left.

recall.q: What is the first test for whether pieces can make a target?
recall.a: The target's square count must be a sum of the piece sizes, for example a multiple of 4 if every piece has 4 squares.

recall.q: Why can a domino tiling fail even when the square count is even?
recall.a: Each domino covers one dark and one light square, so a board with unequal colour counts cannot be tiled.

recall.q: Can a piece be rotated when assembling a target?
recall.a: Yes. It can be turned but not resized.

recall.q: A square is cut into two parts and one part is shown. How do you find the other?
recall.a: Remove the shown cells from the whole square. What remains is the other part, so match its outline against the options.

practice.stem: The pieces are a $2\times 2$ block and a $1\times 6$ bar, and either may be used any number of times, turned in any way, with no overlap. Which rectangle cannot be built from them?
practice.explanation: Each piece covers an even number of squares (4 or 6), so any built rectangle has an even area. The areas are 12, 24, 16 and 15, and only $5\times 3$ is odd. The others work: two bars make $6\times 2$, four bars make $6\times 4$, and four blocks make $4\times 4$. The $4\times 4$ option tempts because the bar cannot fit inside it, but the blocks alone fill it.

lesson.summary: Count squares first and reject targets that are not a sum of piece sizes, then use a chessboard colouring for domino-like pieces, and confirm a buildable target by placing the pieces.

topics.title: Three-dimensional patterns: views, stacks and rolling cubes
points: A solid is described by three orthographic views: top (plan), front and side. A stack of unit cubes is only partly fixed by its views, so questions ask for the minimum or maximum number of cubes consistent with them.

For a stack on a grid, the maximum count puts in each occupied cell of the top view the smaller of the front-view height of its column and the side-view height of its row; the minimum uses as few columns as possible to reach each required height.

A plane slicing a cube can give a triangle, a square, a rectangle, a trapezium, a pentagon or a hexagon; the hexagon is regular when the plane passes through the midpoints of six edges, perpendicular to a body diagonal.
A cube rolled across a grid turns 90° about a bottom edge with each step; track only the top and one side face, writing down which face moves where at every roll.
Folding a net into a cube is the same as rolling a cube across the net: the face that touches each square of the net becomes that square's face.

lesson.why: Solid-shape questions ask which stack of cubes matches a front and top view, or how many cubes a stack can have, and both reduce to reading heights from the views.
lesson.intro: Picture cubes of one size stacked on a square floor grid. A stack is described by a height map: the number of cubes on each floor cell. From the front you see, for each column, only the tallest stack in it, because lower cubes hide behind it. From the side you see the tallest stack in each row. From above you see which floor cells have at least one cube. Edges drawn inside a view mark where neighbouring faces sit at different heights or depths. A smooth object such as a ball has no such edges, but it can still bulge in some places and dip in others.

definitions.meaning: The number of cubes standing on each cell of the floor grid.
For each column, the height of its tallest stack.
Seen from outside, a surface that bulges towards you, like the outside of a ball.
Seen from outside, a surface that dips away from you, like the inside of a bowl.
A line inside a view. Cells in one face have equal height, and cells in different faces have different heights.

principle.text: With column heights $c_j$ from the front view and row heights $r_i$ from the side view, each cell can be at most $\min(c_j,r_i)$ high, so the maximum cube count adds these minima. The minimum count puts a tall stack where a column and a row need the same height, so one stack serves both.

lesson.limits: The views must be consistent: the tallest column height must equal the tallest row height. The minimum has no single formula, so build it by letting one stack serve a column and a row together. These rules assume every cell of the grid may hold a stack; the top view removes the empty cells from the sum. To match a drawing of a stack to its views, the maximum and minimum are not enough: use the face lines, which fix which neighbouring cells are equal in height and which differ.

example.problem: On a $3\times 3$ floor, the front view shows column heights 3, 1, 2 from left to right, and the side view shows row heights 2, 3, 1 from back to front. Find the largest and the smallest number of cubes.
steps: Each cell is at most the smaller of its column height and its row height. The back row (height 2) gives $2+1+2=5$, the middle row (height 3) gives $3+1+2=6$, and the front row (height 1) gives $1+1+1=3$.
The maximum is $5+6+3=14$.

For the minimum, put a stack of 3 where column 1 meets the middle row, a stack of 2 where column 3 meets the back row, and a stack of 1 where column 2 meets the front row. Each stack serves one column and one row, so the total is $3+2+1=6$.
example.result: At most 14 cubes and at least 6.

misconceptions: A view shows the tallest stack, not every stack, so a short stack behind a tall one is invisible and cannot be counted from the view.
Smooth does not mean convex everywhere. A smooth object such as a doughnut has no edges or corners, but it is convex on its outer rim and concave around the hole.
Two cells that look alike in a view are not necessarily at the same height. Only a missing line between them says they are in one face and so equal in height.

recall.q: What does the front view of a stack of cubes show?
recall.a: For each column, the height of its tallest stack.

recall.q: What is the largest possible height of the cell where column $j$ meets row $i$?
recall.a: The smaller of the column height and the row height.

recall.q: How do you reach the minimum cube count?
recall.a: Let one stack satisfy a column and a row together, so each required height is built only once.

recall.q: What does a line inside a view tell you about the two cells it separates?
recall.a: They are in different faces, so their heights differ. Cells with no line between them are in one face and have equal height.

practice.stem: A stack of cubes stands on a $3\times 3$ floor. The front view shows column heights 1, 3, 2 from left to right, and the side view shows row heights 3, 3, 1 from back to front. What is the largest number of cubes the stack can have?
practice.explanation: Each cell is at most the smaller of its column and row heights. Column 1 gives $1+1+1=3$, column 2 gives $3+3+1=7$ and column 3 gives $2+2+1=5$, so the maximum is 15. The tempting answer is 18, from multiplying the sum of column heights by 3 rows, but a row of height 1 cannot hold stacks taller than 1.

lesson.summary: Read column and row heights from the views, bound each cell by the smaller of the two, add for the maximum, and let one stack serve a column and a row together for the minimum.

formulas.name: Reflection in the coordinate axes
formulas.note: Reflecting in both axes in turn is the same as a 180° rotation about the origin.

formulas.name: Reflection in y = x and y = −x
formulas.note: For y = −x both coordinates swap and change sign; forgetting one sign is the usual slip.

formulas.name: Rotation about the origin
formulas.text: 90° anticlockwise (x, y) → (−y, x); 90° clockwise (x, y) → (y, −x); 180° (x, y) → (−x, −y)
formulas.note: Check with (1, 0): 90° anticlockwise must send it to (0, 1).

formulas.name: Net rotation and clock positions
formulas.text: θ clockwise ≡ 360° − θ anticlockwise (mod 360°); hour marks moved = θ / 30°
formulas.note: Add clockwise turns and subtract anticlockwise ones, reduce mod 360°, then convert.

formulas.name: Scaling about a centre
formulas.tex: P' = c + k(P-c),\qquad L' = kL,\quad A' = k^2A,\quad V' = k^3V
formulas.text: P′ = c + k(P − c); L′ = kL, A′ = k²A, V′ = k³V
formulas.note: Translation after scaling does not change area, so only k matters for the area of the image.

formulas.name: Two reflections compose to a rotation or a translation
formulas.tex: \sigma_{m}\circ\sigma_{\ell}=\begin{cases}\text{rotation by }2\alpha & \ell,m\text{ meet at angle }\alpha\\ \text{translation by }2d & \ell\parallel m,\ \text{distance } d\end{cases}
formulas.text: reflect in ℓ then m = rotation by 2α (lines meet at angle α) or translation by 2d (parallel lines d apart)
formulas.note: Reflections in the x-axis and y-axis meet at 90°, so together they make a 180° rotation.

formulas.name: Symmetry of a regular polygon
formulas.text: regular n-gon: n lines of symmetry, rotational order n, smallest angle 360°/n

formulas.name: Mirror image of a clock
formulas.text: actual time = 11:60 − time seen in the mirror
formulas.note: Equivalently 12:00 − t. The rule is its own inverse, so it converts in both directions.

formulas.name: Painted n × n × n cube
where: cubes with exactly k painted faces
formulas.note: Valid for n ≥ 2; for n = 1 the single cube has 6 painted faces. The four counts must add to n³.

formulas.name: Painted a × b × c cuboid
formulas.note: Needs a, b, c ≥ 2. For 4 × 5 × 6: 8, 36, 52 and 24, adding to 120.

formulas.name: Pieces from straight cuts of a block
where: cuts parallel to each pair of faces
formulas.note: Assumes the pieces are not restacked between cuts.

formulas.name: Euler's formula for polyhedra
formulas.note: Holds for every convex polyhedron; pair it with 2E = total sides of all faces to find a missing count.

formulas.name: Edges from faces
formulas.text: 2E = sum of the number of sides of all faces
formulas.note: For 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons: 2E = 60 + 120, so E = 90 and V = 90 − 32 + 2 = 60.

formulas.name: Opposite faces of a standard die
formulas.note: Applies only when the question says the die is standard; otherwise deduce opposites from the views.

formulas.name: Holes after folding and punching
formulas.tex: H = h\cdot 2^{k}\ \text{(away from creases)},\qquad H = h\cdot 2^{k-1}\ \text{(on the last crease)}
formulas.text: H = h·2^k away from creases; H = h·2^(k−1) for holes on the last crease
formulas.note: Two holes that land on the same spot after unfolding count once; unfold step by step when holes sit on creases.

formulas.name: Pieces from one cut across a folded strip
where: half-folds of the strip in the same direction
formulas.note: The cut must cross every layer and miss the creases. A cut along a fold line instead makes fewer, larger pieces, so trace layers.

formulas.name: Creases from repeated half-folds
where: number of half-folds in the same direction

formulas.name: Squares and rectangles in an n × n grid
formulas.note: A rectangle is fixed by choosing 2 of the n + 1 vertical lines and 2 of the n + 1 horizontal lines.

problemTypes.title: Painted cube or cuboid cut into unit cubes
recipe: Identify n (or a, b, c) and which faces were painted.
Classify the small cubes by position: corner, edge interior, face interior, core.
Apply the counts 8, 12(n − 2), 6(n − 2)², (n − 2)³ and check they add to n³.
problemTypes.trap: Using n instead of n − 2 for edge and face cubes, or reusing the all-faces formula when one face was left unpainted.

problemTypes.title: Opposite face from two or three views of a die
recipe: Collect every number seen next to the target; four distinct neighbours fix the opposite face as the sixth number.
With one common face, list both views clockwise from it and pair the numbers in matching positions.
Use the sum-7 rule only if the die is stated to be standard.
problemTypes.trap: Treating two numbers in the same view as possible opposites; faces visible together are always adjacent.

problemTypes.title: Which cube folds from a given net
recipe: Mark the opposite pairs: alternate squares in a straight run, end squares of a Z-shaped four.
Reject any option that shows two opposite faces side by side.
For the survivors, check the cyclic order of the three visible faces around their common corner.
problemTypes.trap: Accepting an option whose visible faces are pairwise adjacent but appear in mirror-image order around the corner.

problemTypes.title: Hole pattern after folding, punching and unfolding
recipe: Write down the folds in order and the final position of each hole.
Unfold the last fold first: reflect every hole across that crease.
Repeat for each earlier fold, merging holes that land on a crease.
Compare the result with the options using its symmetry about the first crease, and about each later crease within the panels that crease joins.
problemTypes.trap: Doubling a hole that lies on a crease; it becomes one hole across the crease, not two.

problemTypes.title: Image of a point or figure under a transformation
recipe: Write the coordinate rule for each step: reflection, rotation, translation or scaling.
Apply the steps in the order stated and test the result on a point such as (1, 0).
For a figure, transform its vertices and compare lengths, orientation and area with the options.
problemTypes.trap: Mixing up the clockwise and anticlockwise 90° rules, or applying a composition in the wrong order.

problemTypes.title: Mirror or water image of letters, words, figures or clocks
recipe: Decide the axis: a mirror reflects left to right, water reflects top to bottom.
For a mirror, reverse the left-to-right order and flip each letter; for water, keep the order and flip each letter upside down.
Letters with a matching line of symmetry look unchanged; for a clock, use actual = 11:60 − shown.
problemTypes.trap: Reversing the letter order for a water image; only a mirror reverses the order.

problemTypes.title: Symmetry counts and whether pieces assemble
recipe: For symmetry, test each candidate line and each rotation of 360°/n separately; they are independent.
For assembly, compare total area first, then try a chessboard colouring to find a parity obstruction.
Allow rotations of pieces, and allow reflections only when the question permits flipping.
problemTypes.trap: Assuming a figure with rotational symmetry must also have a line of symmetry, as with S or a parallelogram.

problemTypes.title: Group figures by rotation, or find the odd one out
recipe: Pick one asymmetric feature of the given figure, such as the short arm of an L or a dot.
Turn each option in the plane until that feature points the same way as in the given figure.
An option that then matches is a rotation; one that matches only after turning over is a mirror image and belongs to the other group.
problemTypes.trap: Grouping a mirror image with the rotations: an L-shape and its reflection have the same cells and outline, but no rotation maps one onto the other.

questions.stem: A 5 × 5 × 5 cube is painted on all six outer faces and then cut into 125 unit cubes. How many of the unit cubes have exactly one painted face?
questions.explanation: One-face cubes sit in the interior of each big face, away from its edges. Each face has a (5 − 2) × (5 − 2) = 9 such cubes, and there are 6 faces, so 6 × 9 = 54. Check: 8 corners + 12 × 3 = 36 edge cubes + 54 + 3³ = 27 core cubes = 125.

questions.stem: The faces of a die are numbered 1 to 6, not necessarily as on a standard die. Two views of the die show three faces meeting at a corner. Read clockwise around the corner, the first view shows 5, 1, 4 and the second shows 5, 2, 6. Which number is opposite 1?
questions.explanation: The common face is 5. Listing both views clockwise from 5 gives 5 → 1 → 4 and 5 → 2 → 6. Numbers in matching positions are opposite, so 1 is opposite 2 and 4 is opposite 6. The remaining number 3 is opposite 5. Option 4 and option 6 are wrong because 4 appears in the same view as 1, and 6 is opposite 4.

questions.stem: Three views of the same die (faces numbered 1 to 6) each show three faces meeting at a corner. Read clockwise, the views show (1, 2, 3), (1, 3, 4) and (6, 4, 3). Which number is opposite 3?
questions.explanation: Every number seen in the same view as 3 is adjacent to 3. The first view gives 1 and 2, the second gives 1 and 4, the third gives 6 and 4. So the neighbours of 3 are 1, 2, 4 and 6, four distinct faces. A face has exactly four neighbours, so the sixth number, 5, is opposite 3. (The views also give 2 opposite 4 and 1 opposite 6.)

questions.stem: The point P(3, −5) is reflected in the line y = −x. What are the coordinates of its image?
questions.explanation: Reflection in y = −x swaps the coordinates and changes both signs: (x, y) → (−y, −x). With x = 3 and y = −5 this gives (5, −3). Check: the midpoint of P and its image, (4, −4), lies on y = −x, and the segment joining them has slope 1, perpendicular to the mirror. (−5, 3) is the reflection in y = x, and (−3, 5) is the 180° rotation.

questions.stem: A figure in the plane is first rotated 90° clockwise about the origin and then reflected in the line y = x. Which single transformation has the same effect?
questions.explanation: Rotation by 90° clockwise sends (x, y) to (y, −x). Reflecting in y = x swaps the coordinates, giving (−x, y). That is the reflection in the y-axis. Check with (2, 5): rotation gives (5, −2), the reflection gives (−2, 5). The composite contains one reflection, so it reverses orientation, which rules out the 180° rotation at once.

questions.stem: A pointer on a clock face points at 3. It is rotated 450° anticlockwise and then 120° clockwise. At which hour mark (1 to 12) does it now point?
questions.explanation: Net rotation: 120° clockwise − 450° anticlockwise = 330° anticlockwise, which equals 30° clockwise mod 360°. Each hour mark is 30°, so the pointer moves one mark clockwise from 3 to 4.

questions.stem: Which of the following words, in capital letters, look exactly the same in their water image (reflection in a horizontal line below the word)?
questions.explanation: A water image keeps the left-to-right order and flips each letter top to bottom, so the word is unchanged exactly when every letter has a horizontal line of symmetry. H, I, D, E, C, O, B and X all do, so HIDE, CODE and BOX are unchanged. In WATER, W, A, T and R are not symmetric about a horizontal line, so it changes.

questions.stem: The reflection of a wall clock in a mirror shows the time as 4:20. What is the actual time?
questions.explanation: A mirror sends each hand at angle θ to 360° − θ, so actual time = 11:60 − 4:20 = 7:40. Check with angles: at 7:40 the minute hand is at 240° and the hour hand at 230°; their mirror positions 120° and 130° are exactly the hands of 4:20.

questions.stem: A square sheet is folded in half left over right, then the result is folded in half bottom over top, then that is folded in half left over right again, giving 8 layers. Two holes are then punched through all layers: one well inside the folded square, and one centred exactly on the folded edge made by the third fold. How many holes does the sheet show when fully unfolded?
questions.explanation: The interior hole passes through 8 separate layers, giving 8 holes. The third fold bends the 4-layer stack, so its folded edge consists of 4 U-shaped bends, each joining 2 layers. A hole centred on that edge cuts each bend once, giving one hole that straddles the crease per bend: 4 holes. Unfolding the earlier two folds reflects these into the four quarters. Total 8 + 4 = 12.

questions.stem: A square sheet with corners at (0, 0) and (4, 4) is folded along x = 2, bringing the left half onto the right half, and then along y = 2, bringing the bottom half onto the top half. A hole is punched at (3.5, 2.5) through all layers. Where are the holes when the sheet is unfolded?
questions.explanation: Unfold the last fold first: reflecting across y = 2 adds (3.5, 4 − 2.5) = (3.5, 1.5). Then unfold the first fold: reflecting both across x = 2 adds (0.5, 2.5) and (0.5, 1.5). The four holes are symmetric about both creases. Option 2 forgets the second fold; option 3 reflects in the diagonals; option 4 reflects the left pair in the wrong line.

questions.stem: A convex polyhedron has 12 pentagonal faces and 20 hexagonal faces, and every edge is shared by exactly two faces. How many vertices does it have?
questions.explanation: Edges: each edge borders two faces, so 2E = 12 × 5 + 20 × 6 = 180 and E = 90. Faces: F = 32. Euler's formula V − E + F = 2 gives V = 2 + 90 − 32 = 60.

questions.stem: A cube net has three rows of two squares each. Row 1 has squares A and B side by side. In row 2, square C lies directly below B and square D to the right of C. In row 3, square E lies directly below D and square F to the right of E. When the net is folded into a cube, which face is opposite A?
questions.explanation: A, B, C and D form a Z-shaped run of four squares (A–B across, B–C down, C–D across). In such a Z, the two end squares become opposite faces, so A is opposite D. By the same rule on B, C, D, E, B is opposite E, and then C is opposite F. B shares an edge with A and C touches A at a corner, so both are adjacent to A, and E and F are already paired with B and C. Folding the net step by step confirms the pairs A–D, B–E, C–F.

questions.stem: Which of the following figures have at least one line of symmetry and also rotational symmetry of order 2 or more?
options: A parallelogram with unequal adjacent sides and no right angle
questions.explanation: H has a vertical and a horizontal line of symmetry and looks the same after a 180° turn (order 2). An equilateral triangle has 3 lines of symmetry and order 3. S and the general parallelogram have order 2, since a 180° turn maps each onto itself, but neither has any line of symmetry.

questions.stem: A long strip of paper is folded in half, the folded strip is folded in half again in the same direction, and this is repeated until it has been folded 4 times. When it is opened out flat, how many crease lines does it have?
questions.explanation: Each half-fold doubles the number of layers, so after 4 folds the strip opens into 2⁴ = 16 equal panels. Panels are separated by creases, so there are 16 − 1 = 15 creases. Fold by fold the new creases number 1, 2, 4 and 8, which also add to 15.

questions.stem: A standard die rests on a table with 1 on top, 2 facing north and 3 facing east (opposite faces sum to 7). It is rolled one step north, tipping over its north bottom edge, and then one step east, tipping over its east bottom edge. Which number is now on top?
questions.explanation: Start: top 1, bottom 6, north 2, south 5, east 3, west 4.
