Rolling north moves the top face to the north side, so the old south face comes up: top 5, north 1, bottom 2, south 6, east and west unchanged at 3 and 4. Rolling east moves the top to the east side and brings the west face up: top 4, east 5, bottom 3, west 2. The top shows 4.

questions.stem: Two diagonally opposite corner squares are removed from an 8 × 8 chessboard, leaving 62 squares. Can the remaining board be covered exactly by 31 dominoes, each covering two adjacent squares?
options: No, because 62 squares cannot be split into pairs of adjacent squares in any board
No, because the two removed squares have the same colour, leaving 30 squares of one colour and 32 of the other
questions.explanation: Colour the board as a chessboard. Opposite corners have the same colour, so the remaining board has 30 squares of that colour and 32 of the other. Every domino covers one square of each colour, so 31 dominoes cover 31 of each, which is impossible. The area condition alone (62 is even) is satisfied, which is why area is not enough to decide.

questions.stem: The triangle with vertices A(1, 1), B(4, 1) and C(1, 5) is scaled by factor 3 about A, then rotated 90° anticlockwise about the origin, then translated by (2, −3). What is the area of the final triangle?
questions.explanation: The original right triangle has legs 3 and 4, so its area is 6. Scaling by 3 multiplies area by 3² = 9, giving 54. The rotation and the translation are isometries and change no area, so the answer is 54. Coordinates confirm it: scaling about A gives (1, 1), (10, 1), (1, 13); the rotation gives (−1, 1), (−1, 10), (−13, 1); the translation gives (1, −2), (1, 7), (−11, −2), legs 9 and 12, area 54. Multiplying by 3 instead of 9 gives the distractor 18.

questions.stem: Figures are drawn on a square grid, each listed as the cells (column, row) it occupies, with rows counted upwards. The given figure is the L-shape {(0, 0), (0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 0)}. Which of the following can be obtained from it by a rotation in the plane, without turning it over?
questions.explanation: Track the foot, the single cell beside one end of the 3-cell bar. In the given L, going up the bar from the foot end, the foot is on the right. Option 1 is a horizontal bar with the foot above its right end: the L turned 90° anticlockwise. Option 4 is a horizontal bar on row 1 with the foot below its left end: the L turned 90° clockwise. Option 2 has the foot to the left of the bar's bottom cell and option 3 has it to the right of the bar's top cell; both are mirror images of the L, which no rotation produces.

questions.stem: A long paper strip is folded in half, then in half again, then in half a third time, always in the same direction. The folded packet is cut once, straight across its width, at a point that is not on any crease. Into how many pieces does the strip fall when opened?
questions.explanation: Three half-folds make 2³ = 8 layers, and the cut crosses all of them, so the opened strip carries 8 parallel cuts at the mirror positions of the cut point. None of them is on a crease, so they are 8 distinct cuts, and 8 cuts across a strip leave 8 + 1 = 9 pieces. The middle pieces stay joined through the creases, which is why the count is not 2 × 8.

questions.stem: Unit cubes are stacked on a 3 × 3 grid, and every cell holds at least one cube. Seen from the front, the three columns have heights 2, 3 and 1 from left to right. Seen from the right side, the three rows have heights 3, 2 and 1 from front to back. What is the largest number of cubes the stack can contain?
questions.explanation: A cell in row i and column j can hold at most the smaller of its row height and its column height. Rows 3, 2, 1 against columns 2, 3, 1 give the grid (2, 3, 1), (2, 2, 1), (1, 1, 1), with sums 6 + 5 + 3 = 14. Every column and row still reaches its stated height, so both views are unchanged. With every cell occupied the least is 12, so the views alone do not fix the count.

pitfalls.text: Confusing mirror and water images: a mirror swaps left and right, water swaps top and bottom. Only the mirror reverses the order of letters in a word.
Treating two faces seen in the same dice view as possibly opposite. Faces visible together always share an edge.
Choosing a folded-cube option that shows two opposite faces side by side. Mark the opposite pairs from the net first, then reject options.
Losing track of layers in multi-fold punching, especially doubling a hole that lies on a crease instead of counting it once per bend.
Rotating 270° clockwise in your head instead of 90° anticlockwise, or adding clockwise and anticlockwise turns without signs.
Applying the sum-7 rule to a die the question never called standard.
Using n instead of n − 2 in the edge and face formulas for painted cubes, or using the all-faces formulas when one face was left unpainted.

errata.claim: The dice example applies the one-common-face rule to "a standard dice" whose views are (3, 1, 2) and (3, 4, 5), concluding that 1 is opposite 4.
errata.correction: On a standard die opposite faces sum to 7, so 3 and 4 are opposite and can never appear in the same view, and 1 is opposite 6. The rule itself is correct, but the example only works for a die numbered arbitrarily, not a standard one.

errata.claim: W, A and T are called horizontally symmetric, which is why they do not change in a mirror.
errata.correction: W, A and T have a vertical line of symmetry, and that is what keeps them unchanged in a mirror. Letters with a horizontal line of symmetry (B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O, X) are the ones unchanged in a water image.
